paragraphs.heading: The cell's power supply
paragraphs.text: Most eukaryotes, including animals, plants and fungi, have organelles called mitochondria in their cells. It has two membranes and uses aerobic respiration to make adenosine triphosphate, or ATP, which the whole cell draws on as a source of chemical energy. Its popular nickname, the powerhouse of the cell, was made widely known by Philip Siekevitz in a 1957 article.

paragraphs.heading: More than energy
paragraphs.text: Mitochondria also take part in signalling, in cells becoming specialised, and in cell death, and they help control the cell cycle and cell growth. They are linked to human conditions such as mitochondrial diseases and heart failure. How many a cell has varies widely: a mature red blood cell has none, while a liver cell can have more than 2000.

paragraphs.heading: Rooms within the organelle
paragraphs.text: In cross section a mitochondrion commonly measures between 0.75 and 3 μm², though size and structure vary a great deal, and it cannot be seen unless stained. It is divided into regions with their own jobs: the outer membrane, the intermembrane space, the inner membrane, the cristae and the matrix. The matrix is the fluid inside the inner membrane. The inner membrane is folded, which gives it more surface area and so raises ATP production.

paragraphs.heading: The outer membrane
paragraphs.text: The outer membrane wraps the whole organelle and is 60 to 75 angstroms thick. It holds many proteins called porins, and a pore-forming protein called VDAC is the main route by which nucleotides, ions and metabolites pass from the cytosol to the intermembrane space and back. Because the outer membrane lets small molecules through freely, the space between the membranes has the same levels of ions and sugars as the cytosol. Larger proteins get in only when a signal at one end binds a translocase, a big protein complex that actively moves them across.

paragraphs.heading: The inner membrane
paragraphs.text: The inner membrane is packed with protein, more than three parts protein to one part phospholipid by weight. Its mix of lipids is unusual: it is rich in cardiolipin, a phospholipid that carries four fatty acids instead of two and may help make the membrane impermeable. Unlike the outer membrane, it has no porins and is highly impermeable to all molecules. Almost every ion and molecule needs a special transporter to enter or leave the matrix.

paragraphs.heading: Once a free-living cell
paragraphs.text: Although most of a eukaryotic cell's DNA is in the nucleus, the mitochondrion carries a genome of its own that resembles bacterial genomes. That finding led to wide acceptance of symbiogenesis, also called endosymbiotic theory. The idea is that free-living prokaryotes, the ancestors of today's mitochondria, fused permanently with eukaryotic cells long ago.

paragraphs.heading: Discovery and name
paragraphs.text: Albert von Kölliker discovered mitochondria in 1857, in the voluntary muscles of insects. Carl Benda coined the name in 1898; it means a thread-like granule.
